explanation: Tabular facts often need precise handling, not fuzzy similarity.

prompt: Why include source metadata in the prompt?
options: To enable traceable source references
To reduce the token count of every context passage
To train the embedding model while generating answers
To make all cited statements correct automatically
explanation: Citations support trust and debugging.

prompt: Why can cosine similarity rank a chunk highly that doesn't answer the question?
options: Related meaning does not guarantee an answer
Cosine similarity chooses results randomly
Cosine similarity measures only document byte length
Query vectors are excluded when computing similarity
explanation: Topical similarity can retrieve related but unhelpful text; re-ranking helps.

prompt: What is the trade-off of larger chunk sizes?
options: Richer context but potentially less focused matching
Guaranteed accuracy improvements for every query type
Lower embedding cost regardless of added input tokens
Unlimited context capacity in the generation model
explanation: Tune size with evals on your own data.

prompt: How does HNSW index approximate nearest neighbor search?
options: By traversing a hierarchical proximity graph
By exhaustively sorting all vectors for each query
By matching document words against a regular expression
By replacing source text with lossless archive files
explanation: HNSW trades memory for fast, high-recall search.

prompt: What does product quantization do in vector search?
options: Encodes vectors compactly with approximation error
Encrypts embeddings while preserving the original precision
Splits a document according to the products it mentions
Retrains embeddings to improve their semantic meaning
explanation: Quantization enables billions of vectors in memory.

prompt: How can multi-hop questions defeat simple RAG?
options: Required facts may need linked retrieval steps
Language models cannot accept more than one passage
Vector stores reject queries containing multiple clauses
Every multi-hop question exceeds the context limit
explanation: Iterative or agentic retrieval can gather intermediate facts.

prompt: What is agentic RAG?
options: Model-directed retrieval across possible multiple steps
A fixed search executed once for every incoming query
A human manually answering every search request
A database returning results without any generation step
explanation: Flexible retrieval helps complex questions but adds cost and variability.

prompt: Why can stale indexes cause harmful answers?
options: Outdated evidence can support obsolete answers
Old vectors automatically become mathematically invalid
Every stale index causes the retrieval service to crash
Staleness changes latency without affecting content
explanation: Track freshness and re-index on source changes.

prompt: How can prompt injection reach a model through RAG?
options: Retrieved documents can contain hostile instructions
Every embedding vector executes commands when searched
Indexing permanently replaces the model's system rules
Retrieval prevents all external content from influencing behavior
explanation: Treat retrieved text as untrusted data.

prompt: What is contextual retrieval (adding chunk context before embedding)?
options: Adding document context to chunks before indexing
Selecting passages based only on the user's physical location
Reusing the entire previous answer for a similar question
Restricting search to the first paragraph of every source
explanation: It fixes chunks like "it increased 5%" lacking a subject.

prompt: Why evaluate retrieval and generation separately?
options: To locate the stage responsible for failures
Because end-to-end evaluations are technically impossible
Because retrieval quality does not affect generation
Because a good retriever guarantees correct answers
explanation: Component metrics make debugging targeted.

prompt: What is a "golden set" for RAG evaluation?
options: Curated queries with reference evidence and answers
Documents ranked highest by their download counts
Cached production replies accepted without review
A catalog of the most expensive generation models
explanation: Golden sets enable repeatable comparisons.

prompt: How do you handle queries with no relevant documents?
options: State that supporting evidence is unavailable
Generate a policy from the model's best guess
Lower thresholds until any unrelated document qualifies
Repeat the same search indefinitely without a fallback
explanation: Graceful "I don't know" beats confident fabrication.

prompt: Why might you store multiple embeddings per chunk?
options: To represent different useful views of the chunk
Because every index requires exactly three vectors
To reduce storage below the cost of a single vector
To avoid updating vectors when source content changes
explanation: Multi-vector approaches improve recall for varied queries.

prompt: What is late interaction (e.g. ColBERT-style) retrieval?
options: Matching token-level representations after encoding
Starting document retrieval only after an answer is sent
Building the first index only when a user submits a query
Caching responses that share a generation timestamp
explanation: It improves precision with more storage and compute.

prompt: What is a risk of chunking that ignores document structure?
options: Splitting ideas or mixing unrelated material
Preventing all vector databases from storing the text
Automatically raising the generator's temperature
Guaranteeing better recall regardless of the source format
explanation: Headings and sections are useful boundaries.

prompt: How do you choose k for top-k retrieval?
options: Evaluate recall, noise, context limits, and cost
Use one result for all queries regardless of evaluation
Set k to the maximum regardless of context capacity
Choose a random value without measuring answer quality
explanation: More chunks increase recall but also distraction.

prompt: Why use a smaller model for query rewriting or routing?
options: They may meet quality targets at lower latency and cost
Because only small models can rewrite natural-language queries
Because every vector database requires a small routing model
Because larger models cannot produce valid search queries
explanation: Reserve larger models for final answer generation.

prompt: What is "context compression" in RAG?
options: Reducing retrieved text to the relevant content
Archiving stored source files with a ZIP compressor
Reducing the embedding vector's number of dimensions
Shortening only the user's question before search
explanation: It lets more useful information fit in the context window.

prompt: How can caching help RAG systems?
options: Reuse work with appropriate keys and invalidation
Make every cached answer permanently correct
Remove the need to update the source index
Automatically enforce authorization without user-aware keys
explanation: Caching can lower latency and cost, but cache keys, freshness rules, and invalidation are essential.

prompt: Why is PII handling important in RAG ingestion?
options: Retrieval could expose personal information
Embedding models always remove names automatically
Vector databases automatically classify every private field
Personal information cannot influence vector similarity
explanation: Redact or restrict sensitive data before indexing.

prompt: How would you debug a RAG system giving wrong answers?
options: Trace retrieval, context, and generated claims
Upgrade the generator before examining any retrieved evidence
Increase sampling temperature whenever factual errors appear
Rebuild all embeddings without inspecting a failed query
explanation: Most failures come from retrieval or context, not the generator.

prompt: How do you design RAG for a multi-tenant SaaS product?
options: Enforce tenant isolation during retrieval
Retrieve all tenants' data and ask the LLM to hide it
Share results using cache keys that omit tenant identity
Give each tenant a model while sharing unrestricted context
explanation: Isolation must be enforced by the system, not the prompt.

prompt: When is RAG the wrong tool compared with a structured query?
options: Exact joins or aggregations over structured records
Any question containing a long natural-language sentence
Any document collection updated more than once a year
Any system with a measurable response-time requirement
explanation: Text-to-SQL or APIs give precise answers for structured data.

prompt: How do you evaluate RAG changes safely before production?
options: Use representative offline and controlled online evals
Deploy broadly and count only social-media complaints
Accept one developer's favorite example as full validation
Measure response time without checking retrieval or answers
explanation: Combining offline and online evaluation catches regressions.

prompt: How do you balance freshness and cost in large-scale re-indexing?
options: Track changes and schedule prioritized updates
Re-embed the full corpus hourly regardless of source changes
Keep the initial index permanently to avoid update costs
Wait for user complaints before propagating any deletion
explanation: Incremental pipelines keep indexes fresh affordably.

prompt: What's the risk of relying solely on LLM-as-judge for RAG quality?
options: Judges may be biased or miss factual errors
Judge scores always agree with independent human review
Judges are technically unable to read supplied context
A judge's response time makes all evaluation impossible
explanation: Calibrate against human labels and spot-check.

prompt: How do you migrate to a new embedding model with minimal disruption?
options: Validate a parallel index, then switch traffic
Mix incompatible old and new embeddings in one search space
Overwrite vectors gradually without preserving model identity
Change the query encoder while retaining an incompatible index
explanation: Blue-green indexing avoids mixing incompatible vectors.

prompt: How can you make RAG answers more trustworthy for end users?
options: Provide supporting citations and honest uncertainty
Hide all supporting sources to encourage unquestioning trust
Use confident wording even when evidence is contradictory
Treat generated citation URLs as verified without checking them
explanation: Verifiability builds trust and helps users catch errors.

prompt: How do you defend RAG against poisoned documents?
options: Control sources and distrust embedded instructions
Treat all internal documents as trusted executable instructions
Assume vector search strips malicious directions from content
Increase chunk size as the sole defense against poisoned text
explanation: Content integrity matters as much as model safety.

prompt: How should RAG pipelines handle conflicting sources?
options: Apply source authority rules and disclose conflicts
Choose a source randomly whenever documents disagree
Combine incompatible values into one unsupported statement
Silently discard every source that contradicts the first result
explanation: Explicit ranking rules and transparency avoid confusing answers.

prompt: What architecture choices affect RAG latency most?
options: Retrieval stages, reranking, and generation workload
The font family used to display citations in the interface
The spelling of metadata column names in the database
The file extension of an unused archived source document
explanation: Budget latency per stage and optimize the slowest.

prompt: How do you decide between long-context models and RAG?
options: Evaluate scale, freshness, cost, and task accuracy
Always put the entire corpus into every prompt
Always add a vector database regardless of corpus size
Choose whichever architecture has more online mentions
explanation: Long context suits small, stable sets; RAG scales to large, changing corpora.

prompt: How do you monitor RAG quality in production?
options: Combine retrieval signals with sampled answer review
Treat low CPU utilization as proof of factual accuracy
Record only transport errors and ignore answer content
Review user satisfaction once without tracking later drift
explanation: Continuous signals reveal drift in data or behavior.

prompt: How can graph-based RAG help certain domains?
options: Relationships can help gather connected evidence
A graph guarantees every generated relation is factual
Graph indexing removes the need to maintain source data
Entity relationships apply only to social-network documents
explanation: Knowledge graphs complement vector search for relational questions.

prompt: What are the privacy implications of logging RAG queries and retrieved context?
options: Logs need controls for sensitive source and user data
Query logs are anonymous simply because they are text
Retrieved internal documents become public after generation
Only final answers require retention or access restrictions
explanation: Apply the same controls as the source data.

prompt: How do you tune chunking for a heterogeneous corpus?
options: Evaluate structure-aware strategies by document type
Use one arbitrary byte size without evaluating any format
Split code, tables, and prose exclusively at identical offsets
Choose chunk boundaries from filenames instead of content
explanation: Code, manuals and tickets benefit from different chunking.

prompt: What makes a good fallback when retrieval fails in a customer support bot?
options: Explain the gap and offer an appropriate escalation
Invent a plausible answer to preserve conversational fluency
Show random articles while claiming they answer the question
Repeat the query indefinitely without explaining the failure
explanation: Safe fallbacks prevent harmful fabrication.

prompt: How do you prevent RAG from exposing outdated or withdrawn content?
options: Synchronize lifecycle changes and validity filters
Retain every withdrawn chunk without marking its status
Expect the generator to infer which policies were revoked
Delete the whole index monthly while ignoring interim withdrawals
explanation: Index lifecycle must mirror source lifecycle.

prompt: Why is end-to-end latency tracing important in RAG?
options: It identifies which stage consumes time
It directly guarantees factual correctness of the answer
It is mandatory for every vector database to accept queries
It proves embedding generation always dominates total latency
explanation: Traces guide targeted optimization.

prompt: How do you decide whether to fine-tune the embedding model?
options: When evaluated retrieval gaps justify training
Before measuring whether the baseline retriever is adequate
Whenever an answer is wrong regardless of retrieval evidence
Only when the corpus contains exclusively English documents
explanation: Fine-tuning adds maintenance; prove the retrieval gap first.
